scope: Audit of original Module 1 text, video, diagram, named examples and citations against the mandatory world tasks and optional NPC teaching. Coverage is judged from teaching propositions, not source-ID presence.

method.readDepth: All original Module 1 JSON blocks and current Module 1 authored beats read. Two original diagrams visually inspected. Two primary TED transcripts fully read. Exact VPRO short-video metadata verified; its transcript unavailable. Primary corroborating papers were generally read at abstract or publisher-excerpt depth, not silently treated as full-text reading.
proofLimits: An optional source film in the library does not teach a proposition in the mandatory game route.
An NPC theory panel supports explanation; optional opening of a panel is not evidence that every learner read or understood it.
This is a content audit. Runtime execution, accessibility, retention, transfer and learning superiority need separate verification.
The VPRO clip remains a hard verification gap. Course text and a related documentary synopsis cannot establish every proposition spoken in the exact short clip.

summary.originalBaseline: Six investigations, 24 authored beats. General moral-economy concepts were present; inequality-policy details and the distinct ecological-growth video were not adequately taught. Several named course cases and citation qualifications were missing or too implicit.
summary.currentAuthoredSnapshot: Eight investigations and 35 beats were present in dist/playbook.json when re-read after supplement integration. The two verified TED omissions and named-case inserts are now present as mandatory teaching tasks. All 16 Module 1 NPC instances have complementary theory panels.
summary.conclusion: Substantially fuller proposition coverage, with specific caveats. Do not claim that every original audiovisual proposition has been verified or that the experience is proven better than the e-learning.
remainingGaps: Exact speech/content of the 60-second VPRO clip mmXGtf6GRjM remains unverified because its caption endpoint returned HTTP 429.
The original bibliography lacks sufficient detail to resolve exact editions or works for Smith 1776/2003, Aalbers 2017 and Kuttner 2019, and does not identify every 2019 Zuboff source precisely.

The complete books and most journal full texts were not read during this audit; broad universal wording in the original course should not be presented as a result directly established by these citations.
NPC explanation panels and additional tasks are authored and statically inspected; this audit does not establish successful learner use or runtime correctness.

media.title: Is inequality inevitable?

readDepth.interval: Original starts at 2:12. Full transcript was read for context; Gini prerequisites occurring earlier are identified as added support, not falsely claimed as part of the played interval.

teachingPropositions.text: Government choices and institutional context affect distribution; historical socialist and capitalist examples show that a single system label does not determine inequality, prosperity or freedom.
Income taxes, inheritance taxes, transfers, education, healthcare and digital access act through different routes.
Wealth and political or media influence can reinforce each other; inequality is not an automatic unchangeable fate.
Gini summarises a chosen distribution and omits several dimensions. Income and wealth must be distinguished.

media.baselineCoverage: m1-05 covered cumulative ownership and conditional r versus g, which did not substitute for these policy mechanisms or counterexamples.
media.implementedAddition: m1-07 contains five teaching beats, a fictional fixed-total transfer exercise and two causal exit slots.
qualifications: Country cards are historical examples from the 2022 film, not current rankings.
No historical inheritance-tax exemption amount is presented as current.
A static transfer changes recipients; it is not a complete growth or behavioural forecast.

teachingPropositions: Human judgement can include empathy, justice, personal beliefs and group norms.
A system's goals and measured variables can omit morally relevant effects.

media.title: Can the economy grow forever?

readDepth.primary: Full published TED transcript read from public page transcriptData translation cues in its Next.js document.
readDepth.copyright: No full transcript copied into the project or this report; propositions are paraphrased.

teachingPropositions.text: Constant percentage growth produces compounding; historical growth motivates a debate over material and ecological conditions.
Economic value differs from physical inputs; labour, capital and resources contribute, and efficiency can reduce inputs per unit.
New demand can offset efficiency gains; ecological damage can matter before physical exhaustion, and feasibility remains contested.
Innovation-driven growth and postgrowth proposals raise distinct evidence, needs, work, public-service and political questions.

media.baselineCoverage: The original game mapped block 21 to an ownership room, but r versus g is not the film's ecological growth question.
media.implementedAddition: m1-08 has five teaching beats, a three-run material calculation, historical-versus-universal claim distinctions and two causal exit slots.
qualifications: Germany's 2000–2014 GDP +16% and CO₂ −12% are explicitly historical film examples.
One country's CO₂ trend does not establish worldwide permanent decoupling of every resource or impact.
Fictional material runs show arithmetic, not a measured demand forecast or an inevitable rebound effect.
Neither growth nor postgrowth is presented as an automatically proven universal solution.

media.readDepth: Full original raster visually inspected, including institutional changes, sector nodes and downstream effects.
teachingPropositions: Deregulation, privatisation and financial priorities are different institutional mechanisms.
Concentration and control over access can affect prices, work, innovation, politics and autonomy.
Named sectors illustrate different possible routes to influence.
media.implementedAddition: m1-05-b7 restores explicit Big Tech, Monsanto/Bayer, Maersk and energy-infrastructure cases.
media.qualification: AI-created diagram contains ambiguous/mistyped labelling. The course's privatisation context takes precedence over a misleading literal label. A schematic is not empirical proof of automatic concentration in every market.

coverageDecisions.content: The verified inequality and ecological-growth propositions require tasks in m1-07 and m1-08. Generic ownership puzzles and library links were insufficient.

Dinner, shared fridge and material-chain settings can change when the same distinctions, reasoning and limits are actually taught. Literal reproduction of every anecdote is not the educational objective.
Named cases are restored while universal or inadequately supported wording is qualified. Understanding a perspective does not require agreeing with every ideological claim.
Original quiz and matching blocks 4, 9, 13, 17, 22, 26, 29, 32 and 34 are assessment evidence. Correct-answer completion alone does not establish initial teaching, comprehension or transfer.

authoredOutputs.placementReason: Distribution and ecological production constraints follow ownership; the final etalage connects production plans to demand and choice architecture.
